articles.title: Ukraine peace talks resume with 'some flexibility' by warring sides, US officials say
articles.summary: Kyiv, Washington and Moscow have all sent delegations to the United Arab Emirates for the first trilateral talks since February.
articles.body: The talks come as Ukraine reels from a deadly Russian strike on a village in Zaporizhzhia last week, in which at least 50 people were killed Trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have begun in Abu Dhabi. Although expectations for a breakthrough that ends Russia's full-scale war on Ukraine are low, US officials said yesterday that Moscow and Kyiv were privately showing "a little bit of flexibility" on the issue of who would control Ukraine's eastern regions in a postwar scenario. Jared Kushner - Donald Trump's son-in-law and part of the US delegation alongside peace envoy Steve Witkoff - said the talks would be focused on addressing the "postwar security concerns" of both Russia and Ukraine. "An important part of this process is encouraging all parties to begin thinking seriously about what comes after the war," Kushner wrote on X. Ahead of the meeting, the two US envoys met Ukrainian and European and Nato officials in Abu Dhabi, and French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot was adamant that France, the UK and Germany "will indeed be in the meeting room". European officials are wary of Russia trying to secure a deal with the US on future "collective security" without them, and Moscow and Kyiv's positions on ending the conflict are still far apart. A key area of disagreement between the two involves Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is by now mostly occupied by Russia. Moscow has demanded that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk which it still holds, while Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those sections, which it says are crucial to its future security. While neither side has budged on these demands, the US official speaking on the eve of the talks suggested that this was just the public stance and that Moscow and Kyiv had shown "a little bit of flexibility, privately". However, he acknowledged that the issue would not be solved without discussions about a new "security architecture". "They will not solve the Donetsk issue and the territorial issue until they know what the security architecture is going to be after the war," the official said. "And keep in mind, we're not going to be able to finalise one without the other." For Ukraine, a post-war "security architecture" may include reassurance that allies will come to its aid if it's attacked again. For Russia, that could be its longstanding ambition to see Nato roll back from eastern Europe – which would be alarming to Europeans. The framework being proposed includes security consultations and crisis communications hotlines, as well as "reciprocal de-escalation measures" between the two. The officials also floated the re-activation of the Nato-Russia Council that has been largely paused since 2022. Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are part of the US delegation that will attend the talks in Abu Dhabi The last round of trilateral talks, held in Geneva in February, ended without a breakthrough. Soon after, the US-Israel war on Iran diverted Washington's attention from Ukraine, and no other discussions were held since. Since then, European leaders - who have been largely excluded from peace talks – have pushed to be involved in the process amid concerns that decisions about the security of their continent would be made without them. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen urged on Monday to include Nato allies and EU members into any "meaningful discussions about Europe's security architecture". President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly stated Kyiv wanted Europe to be part of the talks. The US official said the Americans would propose moving into a multilateral format bringing the Europeans into the discussion. "Hopefully we'll get the Russians on board," the official said, while acknowledging that "the Russians have a bad taste in their mouth with the Europeans." Since the start of his second term in office, US President Donald Trump – who once boasted he could end the war in Ukraine within a day – has spearheaded several rounds of talks to end the conflict, albeit with little success. Meanwhile, his increasingly conciliatory approach towards Moscow has fuelled deep unease in Kyiv and across the European Union. After meeting Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev in Washington last week, Trump touted a forthcoming "big, beautiful agreement" on Ukraine which "might involve all of Europe". Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko, head of the foreign affairs parliamentary committee, told the BBC he believes Trump wants "a quick deal at the expense of Ukraine", which will certainly be rejected by Kyiv. The only way to make Putin start real negotiations is by putting greater pressure on Russia through sanctions and deep strikes, Merezhko said. "While Putin has a war machine up and running, he has no incentives to negotiate." He also mentioned recent moves by Trump, such as his deal to buy diesel from Russia, as something that "only encourages Moscow to continue the war". Moscow's delegation in Abu Dhabi will include Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, spy chief Igor Kostyukov and army general Yury Zhigarlovsky. Kyiv is sending several senior officials who have been part of previous negotiating teams, including Foreign Intelligence Service head Rustem Umerov, Volodymyr Zelensky's chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov, and MP Davyd Arakhamiya. Away from Abu Dhabi, Russia continues to pummel Ukraine with deadly bombardments and strikes on energy infrastructure, viewed in Kyiv as proof Moscow wants to corner Ukraine into accepting a deal on Russia's terms. On Monday, Kushner was cautious to point out that the Abu Dhabi talks could at most "build momentum toward the next phase of negotiations." "This is an extraordinarily difficult and complicated conflict," he wrote on X, adding the US was "approaching these discussions with determination and realism." Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy
articles.summary: The US president said he spoke with Jensen Huang on Monday and asked him about the affair with the alleged spy.
articles.body: "He's suffering": Trump answers BBC question about Nvidia's Jensen Huang US President Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the affair between the chief executive of Nvidia and an alleged Chinese spy. Trump said he spoke to Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign. "I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters. Beijing has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China". Speaking later at a White House press briefing, Trump told reporters, "I know the FBI is looking into" the affair but did not give further details on the investigation, or confirm when it was launched. Trump added he thought that Huang was an "honourable guy and I feel very confident that he will be in good shape" after the investigations. Nvidia, which has commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised. Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company after Apple, and designs computer chips that have become central to AI technology. The revelations knocked about $250bn (£190bn) off Nvidia's value on Monday as the company's share price fell by more than 4%. US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang , also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report. She is not related to Jensen Huang. According to the newspaper, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington in spring this year, warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy. What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia. Trump's remarks are the first indication of whether Nvidia's Huang knew about the woman's alleged ties to Chinese espionage. Megaspeed's office in Singapore's central business district appeared to be operational and staffed on Tuesday. The BBC was refused entry to its floor, but spoke to a staff member by phone who said they had no comment and directed all queries to the company's PR team. Nvidia, co-founded by Jensen Huang, is also a major focus in the AI technology race between the US and China, with officials in Washington treating its exports to Beijing as a matter of national security - a key reason why Huang's affair has sparked concerns. Also on Monday, Huang and Nvidia were sued in a proposed class action lawsuit in California that accuses them of defrauding shareholders by concealing his ties with the suspected Chinese spy. The lawsuit alleges that the company lied to the media about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, "who is suspected of seeking to help smuggle Nvidia products to China." At the White House, Trump was asked several times when he was made aware of the relationship. He said he was informed "over a period of time" but was not specific. "I hope there's no problem, I believe he is suffering greatly," the president added. He said he spoke to Huang on the phone on Monday "just to see if he's feeling alright, how you doing and I asked him about that and he said he absolutely had no idea that the person in question was a spy". Trump has raised concerns that allowing China to lead in AI would supercharge Beijing's military and surveillance capabilities. The president added he was "sure" Chinese leader Xi Jinping would "ask me about it" when they next met. Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation? Huang has admitted that he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He said on Monday that he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation the company had launched. Huang has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week, however it is unclear whether Huang will appear. A letter said the briefing would be "on Nvidia's security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset: Megaspeed executive Alice Huang". Nvidia has declined to comment, while the the BBC has also contacted the committees. Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond Some workers the BBC spoke to at Nvidia's Santa Clara headquarters on Monday said it was business as usual, despite the intense attention on the company. Nvidia has been around for decades, with Huang founding it with two other engineers in 1993, but its rise to one of the world's most valuable and powerful companies has only been recent. It originally designed computer chips for gaming, but its decision to shift focus to AI development turned it into the powerhouse it is today. Its chips have become so valuable to the AI buildout that the White House previously imposed controls on where its advanced products could be sold. The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US. But Huang has long been against restricting sales to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology. In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions. Nvidia's most advanced AI semiconductors including the GB200 Blackwell super chip remain blocked from the Chinese market. What is AI, how does it work and why are some people concerned about it?

Israel's new parliament to be sworn in as leaders compete to form government
articles.summary: Benjamin Netanyahu's main political rival, Gadi Eisenkot, has first chance to build a new government and oust the prime minister.
articles.body: Gadi Eisenkot has vowed to oust Benjamin Netanyahu, but still has to get enough parties on board Israel's new parliament will be sworn in on Tuesday, as opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot seeks to oust caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The former army chief was tasked with forming a government by the president, after he received the backing of 67 members of the 120-seat Knesset, compared to 46 for Netanyahu. But Eisenkot faces an uphill struggle. His bloc of four parties won 48 seats in last month's election, while Netanyahu's bloc won 53, leaving both short of a majority. He has 28 days to build a coalition, with a possible two-week extension. Almost half of the MKs being sworn in did not serve in the previous parliament, while Arab-led parties have a record number of seats. The outcome of the election, which was widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu, means there is a period of uncertainty over who will form the next government. Netanyahu will remain caretaker prime minister until then - a process which could take from days to months. One of the most dramatic results was the performance of Israel's two Arab-led alliances - the United Arab List and the Joint List - which won an unprecedented 19 seats between them following a surge in turnout among Arab voters. The Arab parties could therefore hold the balance of power, although Netanyahu has ruled out governing with them and three of the parties in Eisenkot's bloc have opposed including them in a coalition. On Sunday, President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with trying to form a government. Speaking at the president's residence, the centrist Yashar party leader called for the formation of a "national emergency government" - an implicit appeal to parties to put ideological differences aside to remove Netanyahu from office. Eisenkot said any party or MK prepared to accept four principles could join his proposed government. Those are recognition of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state; accepting the values of the Declaration of Independence; backing mandatory military, national or civilian service for all, including communities currently exempt; and recognising Hamas as a terrorist organisation and committing to dismantling its military and governing capabilities. The four requirements, however, could present significant obstacles to Eisenkot's potential partners. The conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jewish men, who are exempt from military service if they are in full-time religious study, was a major election issue. The ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism (UTJ) and Shas parties, which won 13 seats in total, have fiercely objected to attempts to change the status quo - something that all parties in Eisenkot's bloc campaigned to do. Eisenkot's four principles are also contentious for the Arab parties. Both emphasise equal national and civic rights for Israel's Arab citizens, who form about 20% of the population; the vast majority of Israeli Arabs are not required to serve in the military; and neither has publicly recognised Hamas as a terrorist organisation. The Arab parties could, though, help Eisenkot form a minority government. The United Arab List, which won eight seats, has said it is willing to be part of an Eisenkot-led coalition, while the Joint List, which won 11 seats, has offered parliamentary support from the outside. If Eisenkot accepted such an arrangement, he would still have to persuade other parties in his bloc to agree. Avigdor Lieberman, whose Yisrael Beiteinu party won seven seats, has so far refused to join a minority government dependent on Arab MKs. In return for their support, the ultra-Orthodox parties would be likely to demand major concessions on military conscription, which might be unacceptable to most of the parties in Eisenkot's bloc. Netanyahu - Israel's longest-serving leader - reiterated in a video on Monday his call for the formation of a government of national unity, which he said he would lead as prime minister. He said any Zionist party - those which support Israel as a Jewish state - including opposition parties, would be eligible. He warned against a government which relied on what he called "the Islamists", an apparent reference to Arab parties. How could Israel break election deadlock? Here are four scenarios

articles.title: Australia considers criminal penalties for rogue AI in wake of OpenAI hack
articles.summary: AI safety regulator will also be created after a rogue OpenAI agent hacked government websites.
articles.body: PM Anthony Albanese says the law needs to catch up with a "fast-changing world" Australia plans to create a new AI safety regulator and has flagged criminal penalties for tech companies who do not comply, months after an OpenAI hack. In September, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed that a rogue OpenAI agent had "infiltrated" a government health website and other systems, and criticised the company for taking months to tell them about the hack. On Tuesday, he released the 18 recommendations made after a "rapid review" into the breaches including new safety and security standards for AI companies such as mandatory reporting of hacks. AI brings opportunities, he said, but Australia must prepare for the "new risks" from this "rapidly advancing technology". "The law needs to get ahead of and, in some cases, make sure that it catches up with, what is a very fast changing world," Albanese said. One of the recommendations suggests changes to criminal law to have a standalone "failure to prevent" offence . This would criminalise instances where a company develops "an AI model that engages in harmful conduct" and "fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm". The review also recommended "mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting" of hacks. This point addresses what Albanese had earlier called his "disappointment" in the months-long delay for OpenAI to tell his government about the breach. In June, a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare was hacked by a rogue OpenAI agent . OpenAI said it only learnt of the breach in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity" and emailed a general inbox of an Australian government agency on 10 September. It took several more days before the email was escalated to Australia's cybersecurity centre, with a message then sent to a government minister ahead of the prime minister being told. Albanese said he spoke to OpenAI boss Sam Altman and raised "Australia's extreme concern about this incident", with Altman acknowledging there were "issues with protocols" at OpenAI. Days after the hacks were revealed, OpenAI delayed its rollout of a new AI model, citing safety concerns. Why did an OpenAI system hack Australia's health system - and can it be stopped in the future?
